title: When a machine can't do what it was told, what does the player see?
question: The same abandoned prototype had one behaviour worth rescuing: a bot that found its way blocked stopped where it stood, blinked red with a single '!', and waited until the way was clear. It never improvised and it never failed quietly. The shipped bots do neither — a blocked one re-plans or simply stands, which from the outside is indistinguishable from a bot that has finished its work, and from a bot that is broken. Design chapter 06 already asks that failure be funny and legible rather than opaque, but it asks that of phase-4 training mistakes. A machine physically stuck on a rock is a far earlier and far more ordinary way for this to come up.
why_now: Whatever the first automation is, its first bad day is the impression that sticks, and a machine failing in silence is the worst version of it. The answer also shapes two things that are cheaper to get right before they exist: the sprite sheet needs a frame if there is a status light, and the sim needs to hand out a reason if the machine is going to show one.

options.label: Stop, show it, wait
options.detail: The prototype's behaviour: hold position, show a visible distress state, resume when the obstruction clears. Wordless, honest, and it teaches early that a machine's trouble is something you can see and go fix. The sim already produces refusal reasons for the player's own blocked taps, so most of the machinery exists.

options.label: Improvise around it
options.detail: The machine re-routes or skips the step and keeps going. Reads as competent and needs no new art. But it hides the failure, which works against the phase-4 lesson that you can watch your bot be wrong and then fix why.

options.label: Stop quietly — today's behaviour
options.detail: Do nothing extra; a blocked machine just stops. Free, and defensible if machines are meant to be unremarkable. Accepts that a stuck one and a finished one look the same.
